deep.reconstruction: This page continues the factor table in E283 (Novi Commentarii 9, 1764), whose aim is to find large primes of the form aa+1 (or (aa+1)/2 for odd a). Euler sieves the a-values arithmetically. Every odd prime p dividing aa+1 is ≡1 (mod 4). For each such p one finds the root r of r^2 ≡ −1 (mod p), and then p divides aa+1 exactly when a ≡ ±r (mod p). He marks those a-values, recording the prime divisors smaller than a. Any remaining cofactor larger than a must be a single prime, because two prime factors greater than a would have a product exceeding aa+1. So the table lists only the prime divisors below a (with multiplicity), and a blank line means aa+1 itself is prime. This page covers a = 232–289. Blank entries are 236, 240, 250, 256, 260, 264, 270, 280, 284. Each of these gives a prime aa+1, e.g. 236 → 55697 and 256 → 65537 = F4. Examples of the omitted cofactor: 232^2+1 = 5^2·2153; 288^2+1 = 5·53·313 (313 > 288, so it is omitted); 233^2+1 = 2·5·61·89 (89 < 233, so it is listed). A notable entry is 239^2+1 = 2·13^4, the identity underlying Machin's formula π/4 = 4 arctan(1/5) − arctan(1/239).
errors: None found. I checked all 58 rows. Rows with fully listed divisors were checked by multiplication. Rows with an omitted cofactor or a blank were checked by testing a^2 ≡ −1 (mod p) for all p ≡ 1 (mod 4) up to the needed bound, or up to sqrt of the cofactor. Every entry agrees with the convention 'list prime divisors < a; blank = aa+1 (or (aa+1)/2) prime', and the blanks match the known list of a with a^2+1 prime (OEIS A005574).

ideas.what: Sieve for factoring a^2+1 over a range of a, using the roots of x^2 ≡ −1 mod p for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), to locate primes of the form a^2+1.
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic-polynomial sieve (sieve of Eratosthenes adapted to n^2+1); precursor of later factor tables of n^2+1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E283), and in his letters to Goldbach
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petropolitanae 9 (1762/63, publ. 1764); Opera Omnia I.3

ideas.what: Implicit lemma: a^2+1 has at most one prime factor exceeding a, so listing the divisors below a determines the full factorization.
ideas.modern_name: Elementary bound on large prime factors of n^2+1
Solution of x^2+1 = 2y^4 (Ljunggren 1942: only x = 1, 239); Machin-type arctangent relation
ideas.where_published: Table entry here; Euler discussed arctangent formulas elsewhere

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct page of Euler's well-known factor table for a^2+1, a known and credited contribution. The 239 = 2·13^4 entry is famous for other reasons and is not commented on here. Nothing unfinished or uncredited appears.
